title: the Rajasuya
hook: Yudhishthira wants to give the sacrifice up; Bhima and Arjuna argue for it, and Krishna tells how Jarasandha was born in two halves

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rajasuya ran into a locked gate: Jarasandha, and the kings in his prison. Your line was a king in Magadha.

Yudhishthira hears about Jarasandha and does something unexpected. He backs down. If even Krishna's people fled from this man, he says, how can we stand against him? Let's give up the sacrifice. Peace is better. It's a startling thing to hear from the man whose father asked for this. Then his brothers speak, one after the other. And Krishna tells a story about how Jarasandha came to be born.
screen: `LET'S GIVE IT UP.` → `THE BROTHERS SPEAK.` → `KRISHNA TELLS A BIRTH STORY.`

segments.voice: Bhima speaks first, and bluntly. A king who never makes an effort, he says, gets worn down like an anthill. Then a plan: Krishna's wisdom, my strength, Arjuna's skill. Together, the three of us can do this. Arjuna argues too: they have the strength and the weapons, so why hold back? Yudhishthira's caution isn't mocked. It's answered. Then Krishna tells where Jarasandha came from. A king of Magadha named Brihadratha had two wives and no son. A sage, Chandakaushika, gave him a single fruit to bring a son. The king divided it between his two wives, so neither would be left out. Each queen gave birth to half a child: one eye, one arm, one leg each. Horrified, the queens had the halves left outside. A rakshasi named Jara found them, and as she picked them up, the halves joined into one strong child. She gave him back to the king. And the text says plainly that his name comes from her: Jarasandha, the one joined by Jara. Why tell this in a war council? The story slows down to show who the enemy is before anyone fights him. And it isn't only a monster's tale. A father who wouldn't leave either wife out. Two mothers who couldn't bear what they saw. A rakshasi who, instead of harming the child, carries him home. Even the enemy has a family story. Tomorrow, the three set out for Magadha, and not dressed as warriors.
screen: `AN ANTHILL WEARS DOWN.` · `ONE FRUIT FOR TWO QUEENS.` · `TWO HALVES, JOINED BY JARA.` · `EVEN THE ENEMY HAS A FAMILY STORY.` · then, large: `THE ONE JOINED BY JARA.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a time you wanted to give something up because it looked too big, and notice what helped, or would have: a plan, a friend, someone who saw your strengths more clearly than you did. If it's still in front of you, picture the next small step, just one.
The Rajasuya. Today, the sacrifice nearly given up, then taken back up, with a plan and a story about the enemy's birth.
Your line: the one joined by Jara. Two halves, made whole by a stranger's hands. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: The story of Jarasandha's birth is told in the Sabha Parva of the Mahabharata, which Hindus read, hear recited and see performed as part of the epic.

chat.says: Why is the villain called Jarasandha? Is it just a name?
options: He was born in two halves, and a rakshasi named Jara joined them into one.
It means born of a mango, since a sage's fruit brought his birth.
It means the unbeatable, a title his own army gave him in battle.
chat.meaning: Brihadratha's two queens each bore half a child. The rakshasi Jara joined the halves, and the text says his name comes from her.

Brihadratha.meaning: a king of Magadha, Jarasandha's father

Chandakaushika.meaning: the sage who gave the king a single fruit

rakshasi.meaning: a female rakshasa; here, one who saves a child

Jara.meaning: the rakshasi who joined the two halves into one child

Jarasandha.meaning: the one joined by Jara, king of Magadha

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Rajasuyarambha and Jarasandha-vadha Parvas (Yudhishthira's hesitation; Bhima's and Arjuna's speeches; the birth of Jarasandha)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm Yudhishthira's wish to give up the sacrifice and his reasoning.
Confirm Bhima's anthill image (a king without exertion wasting like an anthill) and his plan of Krishna's policy, Bhima's strength and Arjuna's skill; confirm Arjuna's speech in substance.
Confirm birth details: Brihadratha, two wives, the sage Chandakaushika, a single fruit (mango) divided, half-bodies, Jara joining them, and the text's explanation of the name.
Retellings vary on how Bhima kills Jarasandha; this day avoids foreshadowing the manner of death.
